            Weighted Bipartite Matching is in ModpL

                                                   Abstract
           The recent paper [CGG+ 26] showed that deciding whether a bipartite graph has a perfect
       matching can be reduced to deciding whether a determinant, whose value may be assigned
       to any sufficiently large field F, equals to zero. In the second part of their work, [CGG+ 26]
       also generalized the algebraic method and proposed an NC algorithm that computes the
       maximum weighted perfect matching of bipartite graphs. However, the method they used
       relies on the positivity of non-zero sum of squares and does not generalize to finite fields.
       In this paper we further leverage their ideas and show that the algebraic method works in
       finite fields as well, therefore maximum weighted perfect bipartite matching is in Modp L.


1     Introduction
Here we briefly present the ideas in [CGG+ 26] and introduce several notions.
    A bipartite graph G = (L ∪ R, E) consists of vertices L ∪ R and edges E ⊆ L × R. We
consider balanced bipartite graphs, that is, |L| = |R| = n. A matching is a subset of E that
covers each vertex of G at most once. A perfect matching is a matching of size n. For an
unbalanced bipartite graph with |L| < |R|, define a left-saturated matching as a matching that
covers L. A weighted bipartite graph consists of G and a weight function w : E → [0, W ] ∩ Z.
Here we let W be a polynomial of n.
    Determining whether a bipartite graph has a perfect matching, and searching for such a
matching, is a classic problem. If a perfect matching exists, we can further ask what is the
maximum weight of a perfect matching. In [CGG+ 26], it is shown that both problems can be
solved in NC. Specifically, deciding whether G has a perfect matching and finding the maximum
weight of a perfect matching can be done in NC2 while searching for a matching can be done in
NC3 . We focus on the two decision problems.
    For the perfect matching problem, they constructed a matrix M (G) of size nD × n2 r so
that M (G) has full row rank iff G has a perfect matching. Here the parameters are set to
D = n(r − δ) where δ ≥ n and r > n2 δ. Roughly speaking, M (G) is a matrix that has slightly
more columns than rows. The construction takes 3 steps:
    1. Let A be the n × n adjacent matrix of G, where Aij = 1 iff (i, j) ∈ E.
    2. Expand A to a n × n2 matrix Â. Here Â = (A | A1 ), where (A1 )i((n−1)i+j) = 1 (1 ≤ j ≤
       n − 1), and the other entries are 0.
    3. Replace each entries of Â with D × r blocks, thus producing M (G). Specifically, replace
       each 0 with 0 matrices, and replace each Âi,j = 1 with γ-folded Vandermonde matrix
       V (αj ). Here γ is an element in F with an order more than D and {αi γ j | 1 ≤ i ≤
       n2 , 0 ≤ j < r} is a set with n2 r distinct elements. The γ-folded Vandermonde matrix
       V (α) = ((αγ i−1 )j−1 )ij . The construction is closely related to subspace designs. (Refer to
       [CGG+ 26], Section 2 and 3 for details.)
